title: Ang 1292–1293: Namdev and Ravidas
hookLine: the temple turned, and the family's work
tomorrow: 1 a.m., boxes everywhere, and a video call from a stranger. who?

cards: Simran's cousin's graduation party: a backyard full of folding chairs and uncles. One of them, holding a paper plate, calls across the table: still driving trucks, Harjit?
Still, her dad says, and laughs, and passes the pakoras. The uncle turns to Simran. Good thing you're going to college, beta.
Her face goes hot. Her dad built that company from one truck. On ang 1292, a singer gets a far worse version of this.
He's thrown out of a temple. And then the temple does something.

teach.h: NAMDEV: THROWN OUT OF THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: The singer is Namdev, a bhagat whose hymns are in the Granth. In his Malar hymn, in paraphrase: calling me low, they struck me and drove me out; what do I do now, Father Vitthal? Vitthal is a name of God he loved.

teach.h: THE TEMPLE TURNS TO FACE HIM.
teach.b: The temple swung around to face Namdev, its back to the ones who drove him out. A building, choosing the singer. On the very next page, ang 1293, Ravidas tells his own family's story without lowering his voice.
In paraphrase: my people carried dead cattle around Banaras, every day. And now the leading Brahmins bow before them, because your servant Ravidas has taken refuge in your Name.
Two bhagats, two kinds of work the world looked down on. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: the Granth doesn't tidy up where these voices came from.
Ravidas names his family's trade himself, and the Gurus kept it in, next to their own hymns.
Sikhs hear in it the honor of kirat, honest work: the hands that carry are not lower than the hands that pray.
Back at the party, Simran doesn't argue with the uncle. She gets up, fills her dad's plate, and pulls her chair around to sit beside him, her back to the uncle. A small temple, turning.

how: Sikhs sing the bhagats' hymns in kirtan as Gurbani; the Ravidas and Namdev hymns at the end of Malar are found under their names after the Gurus' hymns and the ballad.

o: where a temple turns to face Namdev
where Guru Nanak's rain ballad begins
where Guru Ram Das opens the night raga

games.q: the end of Malar — tap the pairs.
p: thrown out; the temple turned to him
the name of God Namdev loved
named his family's work in his hymn
honest work, not lower than prayer

s: Ravidas hides his family's trade in his hymn
he names it himself: his people carried dead cattle around Banaras.
in Namdev's Malar hymn, the temple turns to face him
its back to the ones who drove him out.
in Sikh teaching, prayer is holy and work just pays the bills
the Granth keeps the singers' trades beside their songs; honest work, kirat, is honored.

games.q: a classmate says his mom's job cleaning offices is embarrassing to say out loud at career day. with Ravidas in mind, what do you tell him?
o: Ravidas named his family's work in a holy book. say it proudly.
pick a vaguer word; nobody needs to know what she does.
some jobs are holier than others, but hers pays the bills.
games.why: Ravidas names his family's trade, carrying dead cattle, in his own hymn, and the Gurus kept it in the Granth. every job is holy.

practice: Bring to mind one job that keeps your day running and rarely gets thanked: a driver, a cleaner, a cook, someone who carries things. Hold that person in mind for the sit, and with each out-breath, quietly thank them.
If you'd like, read ang 1293 first.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1292. Where Namdev and Ravidas sing in Malar: a temple that turns, and a family's work named without shame.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dehura, a temple; in Namdev's hymn it turns to face him.

carryVoice: Your line: every job is holy, and the Granth kept the singers' trades. Day sixteen hundred four, done.
